stories.title: a room is a place
stories.moment: Callum sent over the second iteration of the scheduler redesign, and I pushed back: the room block needed to read as a wall, not a card. He tried solid fills. I said yes. Then he stopped and wrote a paragraph I wasn't expecting. "A room is a place and an appointment is a promise and we were treating both as boxes." A place is persistent, has a location, can be empty. A promise is conditional, temporary, belongs to people. So the room should be a column that exists whether anything is scheduled or not. I wrote back: "this is the smartest thing anyone has said about this product."
stories.why_it_matters: The reframe came after the solution, not before.

stories.title: twenty-eight days to pay an invoice
stories.moment: Callum sent his invoice to Dane's email on April 20. I redirected him to accounting@thicket.vet, an address that hadn't existed when he signed the contract. He resent it. Eighteen days later he checked in, apologetic: Stripe usually hits by now. I didn't see it for a day. Then I found out the PO number didn't match our system, asked him to resend with a new format Dane had implemented without telling anyone. He pointed out he'd copied it from last month's invoice. Fourteen days after that he wrote again: rent was the next day and he was short. Dane had left it in approvals, didn't realize the new bank account required two signatures. I pushed it through.
stories.why_it_matters: Each delay was someone else's process change he had no way to anticipate.

stories.title: Westbrook migrated without telling anyone
stories.moment: Dane checked the database and found that Westbrook had quietly moved all their historical records into the system. They hadn't announced it, hadn't asked for help, just did it. He messaged me asking if we should call them. I told him to wait a week and see if they actually used it. Five days later they came back asking about pricing, which meant they were in. The silence before the migration was the tell—they were deciding whether to commit, and the answer came as data in the database, not words in an email.
stories.why_it_matters: The conversion happened in the gap, not on a call.

stories.title: He bought the booth before asking
stories.moment: Dane found a 10x10 booth slot at the VMX conference in August, next to Purina, for $2400. He wrote that it was "actually perfect" because every clinic owner in the northwest would be there. Then he sent two more messages: "i kind of already told them we'd take it" and "sorry." I wrote back "ok" and that was it. No argument, no breakdown of whether we had the cash or whether the timing made sense. He'd committed us and apologized in the same breath, and I let it go.
stories.why_it_matters: The apology arrived after the decision, not before.

stories.title: Three weeks of asking about Nkechi
stories.moment: Dane asked on the 9th whether we'd heard back from Nkechi, the engineer we were trying to hire. I said I'd ping her that week. Thirteen days later he asked again: "so are we hiring her or." He wrote that he needed to know because "the billing conversation changes a lot if it's you and callum vs you and an actual engineer." I wrote back "still talking to her" and nothing else. No timeline, no update, no acknowledgment that two weeks had passed since I'd said I'd follow up. He was asking whether to plan around a hire and I gave him the same non-answer twice.
stories.why_it_matters: Each answer confirmed the question would get asked again.

stories.title: Failure stories are more useful than success stories
stories.moment: Marguerite signed the investment documents and immediately made three requests. The third one stuck: she offered to introduce me to two people who had tried to sell software into independent practices and failed at it. I wrote back that this was "the single most useful offer anyone has made me this year" and I meant it literally. She responded the next morning with a one-liner: "'One is real and two are polite' is a better summary than most seed decks manage." Six days later she sent both introductions with enough context that I knew exactly what to ask each person. One had shut down scheduling software for equine practices after eighteen months. The other had tried to sell practice management to dental offices and hit the same front desk problem I was starting to suspect we had.
stories.why_it_matters: The request came before the money cleared, not after the first problem.

stories.title: I did not answer the third question
stories.moment: Marguerite asked three questions about the pilots in mid-May. I answered the first two in detail: the rewrite took eleven days, Rosalind was still logging in daily, the polite pilots had gone quiet. The third question was whether anyone was paying me yet. I sent the May update two weeks later without addressing it. She wrote back on June 8th with nine words: "I do not think you answered the third question." I wrote two days later and admitted that nobody was paying, that I'd been "reluctant to put a number in front of Rosalind while the product was still doing the thing that nearly lost her," and that I knew this reason would become an excuse around July. Fifteen days later she replied that I had now told her twice I would have an answer after a conversation I had not yet scheduled.
stories.why_it_matters: The gap between when the question was asked and when it was answered is the story.

She was gentle on the phone, then sent an email saying she'd been too gentle, that she'd survived three practice management systems and chose us because we asked better questions, but she could not have her surgical tech navigating around the software to keep a dog safe. I spent the weekend rebuilding the scheduler so rooms could be reserved with no client attached. Told her two weeks. She wrote back: "That's the right answer, and the two weeks is the part that tells me it's the right answer."

stories.title: The bathroom floor dried on its own
stories.moment: Ezra sent three separate emails in three days about standing water in the rear bathroom. The first assured me it was not a plumbing issue but a 'drainage characteristic' of the building's original construction. The second confirmed the water level had decreased and he'd added a mat. The third announced the floor was now dry, 'as indicated,' and that if water appeared again it would 'resolve naturally within 24 to 48 hours.' I sent one reply in the entire sequence: 'Got it, thanks for looking into it.'
stories.why_it_matters: The problem fixed itself, but the correspondence kept going.

stories.title: Washing hands too enthusiastically
stories.moment: The bathroom flooded again. Ezra wrote to say the cleaning service had found water on the floor, and this time he had a theory: excessive water usage at the sinks, paper towels disposed of improperly, mats not used as intended. I asked if the floor was flooding because we were washing our hands too enthusiastically. He replied the next day to clarify it was not 'flooding' but 'water accumulation due to usage patterns,' and that the distinction was important from a liability perspective. The sink basin was shallow, the faucet pressure commercial-grade, and 'when used without attention to splashing' water exited the basin perimeter. I wrote back to say we would be more careful. Three days later he documented the exchange and noted that if the issue recurred, 'we may need to revisit the facilities clause in your lease agreement.'
stories.why_it_matters: One question about handwashing became a lease violation threat in under a week.

stories.title: A simple agreed or confirmed will suffice
stories.moment: After 'yesterday's incident,' Ezra sent a numbered list of tenant responsibilities for the shared bathroom: paper products disposed of appropriately, personal items removed within twenty-four hours, no storage of cleaning supplies. I replied 'Acknowledged.' The next day he wrote back to say he needed explicit confirmation that Thicket agreed to observe points one through five as stated, and that 'a simple agreed or confirmed will suffice.' I sent: 'confirmed.' He replied again to say he had filed my confirmation and would refer back to it should any future incidents occur.
stories.why_it_matters: Each reply I sent became the reason for another message asking for more.

stories.title: The venmo that never came
stories.moment: Wendy found a shop in Berkeley that restores old radios and wanted to split the cost for their mom's sixtieth. I said yes and told her I'd venmo her that week. I did not venmo her that week. Three weeks later she brought it up again, opening with "not chasing you for it," which meant she absolutely was chasing me for it but did not want to make me feel bad. She said she just didn't want Rahul to think she'd forgotten to ask. The thing she was protecting was not the money, it was whether someone else would think she'd dropped something.
stories.why_it_matters: The apology is always for someone else's impression, never for the actual delay.

stories.title: Let me look at the calendar
stories.moment: Wendy asked if I could come the Friday before the party to help with the cake, the chairs, and the tent. She wrote that it would be really nice to not do this by herself. I told her I would look at the calendar that week and get back to her. I did not get back to her. Nineteen days later she wrote again. She opened by saying she knew I was busy, that she wasn't saying it in a pointed way. Then she said the tent people needed a final count by Monday, and asked, "I'd just like to know if I should set a place for you." The shift from "can you help on Friday" to "should I set a place for you at all" arrived without an argument in between.
stories.why_it_matters: The ask scaled down each time, and the thing that changed it was silence.

hero_line: Ten messages across eight weeks, and both times the thread went quiet I was the one who wrote first.

timeline.title: Billing is a trapdoor
timeline.description: I asked whether to build billing and he said no, the problem was why two customers weren't using what we'd already built.
timeline.evidence: Billing is a trapdoor. Don't.

timeline.title: I defended the features list

timeline.evidence: Fair enough. Good luck with it.

timeline.title: Twenty-three days, then I wrote first

timeline.title: Thirty days, then I asked about services

timeline.title: The twenty-implementation cap, written down
timeline.description: He told me the argument was better than he expected but the rule only worked if I wrote the number where Dane could see it.
timeline.evidence: Rules you keep in your own head aren't rules.

stories.title: That's a features list, not a product
stories.moment: I asked whether to build billing, since two clinics had asked for it and Dane thought it would close the seed. Theo sent back one line: "That's a features list, not a product." He pointed out that one of our three customers was actually using the thing we'd already built, and asked why nobody had checked on the other two. I wrote back the same day with reasons—paper records, a retiring front desk manager—and said neither was a product problem. He replied the next morning with six words: "Fair enough. Good luck with it." Twenty-three days later I told him we'd cut billing and that the front desk manager had been a product problem all along. I'd built for her replacement without noticing I was making that decision.
stories.why_it_matters: The concession came three weeks late and only after the thing I defended had failed.

stories.title: Twenty implementations, then we stop
stories.moment: I wrote to Theo about whether to do implementation services, not because the software was hard but because every customer's process was a mess and the software made it legible for the first time. I said we'd stop at twenty implementations, once we'd learned enough to build a product that installs itself. He wrote back that it's "the thing everybody says at ten" and that the stop only holds if replacement revenue already exists, otherwise you're choosing between your rule and payroll. I pushed back: if twenty implementations produce a product that installs itself, the replacement revenue isn't a bet, it's the output. Three days later he conceded: "That's a better argument than the one I was expecting." Then he told me to write the number down somewhere Dane could see it, because "rules you keep in your own head aren't rules."
stories.why_it_matters: The rule only became real once it stopped being private.

prep.last_substantive_interaction: I argued that capping services at twenty implementations would force us to build a self-installing product. He said that was better than he expected and told me to write the cap down where Dane could see it.

stories.title: per-seat pricing was fear, not strategy
stories.moment: Josiah sent unsolicited notes on the pricing page after showing Thicket to someone as an example. He pointed out that per-seat pricing punished the exact people who used the software most: a two-vet clinic had eleven people touching the schedule but only two generating revenue, so the front desk became a cost center. I wrote back at 11pm and admitted the whole model existed because it was the thing I understood how to build. I'd been calling it a pricing strategy for four months. He also flagged a FAQ line that I'd written to preempt an objection I was afraid of. I told him it was "just fear written down" and deleted it. He got me an intro to a pricing consultant the next morning.
stories.why_it_matters: The admission arrived twelve hours after the critique, at night, with no cushioning.

stories.title: hired for domain, wrong for two months
stories.moment: I asked Josiah whether domain background mattered for a first engineering hire. The candidate I wanted most had no healthcare experience. The two who did were both fine and neither was her. He said he'd cared a lot about domain and had been wrong. His domain hire moved faster for ten weeks, then plateaued, because the hire kept building how the industry already did things. The person who didn't know anything "asked why four times a day and two of those questions were good. One of them changed the product." Then he reframed the whole question: did I have the hours to be her domain for two months. I wrote back the next day and said I didn't have the hours, but I'd rather find them for the right person than not need them for the wrong one.
stories.why_it_matters: The question I asked was not the question that mattered.

stories.title: the intro I never sent
stories.moment: Josiah asked for an introduction to Marguerite Vance, who'd led my round and kept coming up as someone who understood the operator side of what he was building. He flagged that intros were a real thing to spend and told me to say no if the timing was bad. I said I'd think about the right framing so it would land, and asked for a few days. Twenty-seven days later he sent a short follow-up with no pressure, offering to draft the blurb himself. Twenty-one days after that he wrote one last time: "If you thought about it and landed on no, genuinely no hard feelings. I'd just rather know than keep wondering whether my email went to spam." I never answered.
stories.why_it_matters: The gap from offer to silence was forty-eight days, all of it on me.

stories.title: The room that was actually two rooms
stories.moment: Beatriz emailed to say she'd entered all five rooms like we'd planned. Then, same day, she sent a second message: Exam 2 and Exam 3 were actually one room with a curtain down the middle. They tracked them separately because they could double-book for exams, but if one side had surgery prep they had to block both. She closed with "figured I should mention it before someone books a neuter on one side and a puppy wellness check on the other." I wrote back five days later to say that mattered a lot and I'd need to think about how to model it without making the interface horrible.
stories.why_it_matters: The thing that breaks the system always surfaces after go-live, not before.
